title: Apple Sues OpenAI, Alleging Stolen Hardware Secrets
hook: Two of tech's biggest names are now suing each other. Apple says former employees carried its confidential hardware secrets straight into OpenAI's push to build its own devices.
key_points: The Verge reports Apple sued OpenAI, alleging theft of Apple's trade secrets to advance OpenAI's hardware plans.
Apple's complaint alleges 'a pattern of theft' by OpenAI employees formerly at Apple.
Ars Technica reports the suit claims one ex-engineer exploited a software bug to obtain trade secrets.
The lawsuit also names IO Products, the hardware startup co-founded by former Apple designer Jony Ive.
The Verge reports OpenAI's hardware lead allegedly asked Apple job candidates to bring in unreleased Apple hardware samples.
It's a sign of how fierce the competition for AI hardware talent — and secrets — has become, with OpenAI's hardware bet now on the line.
content_html: The race to build the next big AI hardware device just turned into a courtroom fight. The Verge reports Apple has sued OpenAI, alleging that engineers who left Apple carried confidential trade secrets with them and used them to advance OpenAI's own hardware ambitions.
extra_html:
Apple's complaint describes what it calls "a pattern of theft" by former Apple employees who joined OpenAI, and the lawsuit also names IO Products — the hardware startup co-founded by celebrated former Apple designer Jony Ive, which has been working with OpenAI on new AI devices. Ars Technica reports one specific allegation: that a former engineer exploited a software bug to get at Apple's confidential material. The Verge separately reports an even more pointed claim from the suit — that when Apple employees interviewed for jobs at OpenAI, the company's hardware lead allegedly asked them to bring in components and unreleased product samples they'd been working on at Apple.

The specifics will get argued out in court, but the bigger picture is easy to read: as AI labs push beyond software into physical devices, they're competing directly with the company that has defined consumer hardware for two decades, for the same specialized talent and know-how. When that competition gets personal enough — engineers moving from one to the other, allegedly with confidential material in tow — it stops being just a race and starts being a legal fight over who actually owns the ideas. The stakes are real for OpenAI too: it's one of several lawsuits the company is now juggling, and it lands squarely on top of its own expensive hardware ambitions.

related.title: Who Controls AI?
related.hook: The most powerful AI models are built by a handful of giant companies, because training them costs a fortune. Who holds that power — and whether 'open' AI can balance it — shapes everything.

related.title: The $400 Million Machine Behind Every AI Chip
related.hook: Every AI chip starts on a machine most people have never heard of: a $400-million, bus-sized contraption from a single Dutch company that the whole industry depends on.
